extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, stakeholders, advocates, and practitioners who submit comments on federal agency rulemakings (including lawyers, policy advocates, and impacted individuals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for participating in federal notice-and-comment rulemaking: the procedural steps agencies follow and practical criteria for drafting effective public comments that agencies must consider and that strengthen legal defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of Proposed Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal first step: the agency must publish a proposed rule in the Federal Register to trigger the comment period and give notice to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Comment Period (timing and eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Usually 30 to 60 days. It can be longer in cases of big rules." Anyone globally can submit; no formal invitation required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the comment window length (commonly 30–60 days) and that any person or organization may file comments; longer windows may apply for complex rules. Timely submission during this period is required for the comment to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency review obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must read and consider all comments (potentially millions for major rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are required to review submitted comments and cannot simply ignore them; however, consideration does not mean automatic adoption of the views expressed. The obligation to consider underpins how agencies respond in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule publication requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency publishes final rule with preamble explaining legal authority, responding to significant comments, and justifying decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule's preamble must identify the agency's legal authority, respond to significant arguments raised by commenters, and provide reasoned explanations for choices—content that is central to defending the rule on judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date standard
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most final rules take effect 30 days after publication unless the agency provides good cause for a different effective date or follows statutory exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific and evidence-based comments
rubrics_metrics.description: "Specific and evidence-based" rather than vague opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should present concrete facts, empirical data, citations, or detailed examples; vague statements of liking/disliking are weak. Provide sources, references, or empirical analysis when possible to make the point persuasive and recordable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on measurable impacts and practical concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be focused on measurable impacts and practical concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe quantifiable effects (costs, safety impacts, operational burdens) and real-world implementation problems. Agencies rely on evidence about practical consequences when evaluating and responding to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise issues the agency may have overlooked
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing overlooked issues the agency may not have considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight factual situations, stakeholder perspectives, or local conditions not discussed in the proposed rule; novel or underappreciated issues increase the chance the agency must explain why they are or are not being addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat comments as a vote
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is absolutely not a vote. The agency isn't doing a poll." The agency is not obligated to adopt majority-supported positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on numeric support alone; instead, provide substantive arguments and evidence. While volume can signal importance, agencies must engage with reasoning and material arguments rather than merely tally preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise legal authority and statutory/regulatory consistency arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that engage with legal arguments (e.g., ADA consistency) and statutory/regulatory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify statutory conflicts, cite relevant statutes/regulations/case law, and explain why the proposed rule is or is not consistent with governing legal frameworks. Agencies are expected to address such legal challenges in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document concrete, case-specific concerns (use technical details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete examples and technical facts (example: "hooves could puncture an aircraft evacuation slide").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, technical, or safety-related facts force the agency to consider and document responses. Use illustrative scenarios, engineering or medical data, or plausible operational examples to make concrete the risks or burdens claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of ossification and agency bypass through guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The process has become so elaborate that agencies sometimes bypass it entirely by issuing non-binding guidance — accountability protections paradoxically reduce accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that agencies may issue guidance instead of formal rules to avoid notice-and-comment. Advocacy strategies should account for the possibility that substantive policy shifts will occur outside formal rulemaking, and consider other accountability tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comment strategy to improve legal defensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must engage substantively with comments and explain their reasoning — a requirement that strengthens legal defensibility on judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame comments to highlight legal weaknesses or evidentiary gaps so the agency must address them in the administrative record; well-documented comments make it harder for the agency to defend arbitrary or inadequately justified decisions in court.
